CH08-M01: A web browser connects to a server and sends an HTTP request. HTTPS adds TLS to protect traffic in transit, but the server still decides who may access each object.
CH08-M02: Requests contain a method, target, headers and sometimes a body. Responses contain a status, headers and a body. A 404 says a resource was not found, not why.
CH08-M03: Headers convey metadata such as Host, Content-Type and cache rules. A header is not proof of identity merely because a client supplies it.
CH08-M04: Servers associate session IDs with authenticated state. Secure, HttpOnly, and SameSite cookie attributes reduce distinct risks, but server-side authorization is still required.
CH08-M05: A configured proxy receives client HTTP traffic and forwards it. HTTPS interception in a test browser usually needs an installed training proxy certificate. Never intercept others.
CH08-M06: Burp Community provides Proxy and Repeater. Configure its browser to visit ONLY the running NULLTRACE 127.0.0.1 training portal, then examine the request safely.
CH08-M07: Repeater lets you resend one HTTP request with a harmless parameter or header changed. Compare both bodies and status codes; document what the difference demonstrates.
CH08-M08: Broken object-level authorization occurs when a server returns another user’s object based on an ID without checking permission. The fictional training portal intentionally demonstrates this.
CH08-M09: The server must verify the current session’s permissions for EACH requested object. Renaming IDs or hiding buttons cannot repair a missing authorization check.
CH08-M10: A responsible web assessment records exact request parameters, observed responses, limitations, impact in the controlled setup, and a realistic server-side mitigation.
CH09-M01: Incident handling covers preparation, detection and analysis, containment, remediation, recovery, and lessons learned. Preserve evidence before making disruptive changes when practical.
CH09-M02: Host, proxy and network logs may use different clocks. Record where each event came from, when it was collected, and whether the source may be incomplete.
CH09-M03: A SHA-256 digest detects changes against a known digest. It cannot establish that the original data was truthful or that its author is who they claim to be.
CH09-M04: Normalize timestamps to one time zone, preferably UTC. A device clock can drift even if timezone conversion is correct, so mark uncertain ordering when appropriate.
CH09-M05: A packet capture shows network activity; a host log shows local activity. A shared timestamp is a clue, not causal proof—correlate connection and process metadata.
CH09-M06: An open TCP port shows a listening service was reachable during a specific scan. An exposure finding requires further context before it is a vulnerability or compromise finding.
CH09-M07: Sanitized request logs reveal URLs, methods, status codes, and identifiers. Handle real authentication tokens as sensitive; this game uses fictional metadata only.
CH09-M08: False positives are expected in security monitoring. Explicitly document competing hypotheses and what new evidence would distinguish routine activity from an incident.
CH09-M09: An incident report separates observations, technical findings, confidence levels, limitations, and prioritized mitigations. Document methods so another analyst can reproduce them.
CH09-M10: The synthetic NEXUS dossier contains MI-07 and summary IS-21 with conflicting claims. The disagreement is real within the fictional evidence, but intent needs corroboration.
CH10-M01: Final investigations need authorized scope, data minimization, retention rules, a clear question, and a plan for verifying each proposed claim.
CH10-M02: A topology combines interface and route configuration with observed reachability. A diagram is a model; label devices and links that are inferred rather than verified.
CH10-M03: The bundled DNS PCAP shows an IP querying mirror.training.invalid. It does not show a page visit or decrypt an HTTPS session.
CH10-M04: Recorded Nmap states include open, closed, and filtered. A filtered state means the scan could not determine a definitive port state because of missing or blocked responses.
CH10-M05: Synthetic password auditing shows how weak passwords are found in tiny dictionaries. The lesson is to improve credential policy and use modern adaptive hashing plus MFA.
CH10-M06: Use the controlled localhost portal and manual HTTP request modification to demonstrate that the server fails to enforce case ownership. Recommend authorization checks on each request.
CH10-M07: When records disagree, preserve originals, verify hashes and timestamps, and report precisely what contradicts what. Do not equate a discrepancy with proof of malicious intent.
CH10-M08: A defensible final dossier identifies source artifacts, preservation method, hashes, normalized times, corroborating findings, alternative explanations, and what remains unknown.
CH10-M09: A disclosure decision weighs accountability, privacy, public risk, operational continuity, and the credibility of the preserved dossier. No path justifies exposing unrelated secrets.
CH10-M10: Use independent packet, scan, credential, HTTP, and incident records to support a bounded conclusion. Select a disclosure route in the Story Archive before submitting the capstone.
